quickAnswer: Nearly all Indian traditions frame the highest goal as freedom — moksha, mukti, kaivalya or nirvana — from bondage to ignorance, craving or karma. They differ on what freedom is and how it comes: knowledge of the Self in Advaita, isolation of consciousness from nature in Sankhya-Yoga, the ending of craving in Buddhism, the shedding of karmic matter in Jainism, and loving union or service through grace in the bhakti schools. The Gita offers several paths — action, knowledge, meditation and devotion — and treats them as converging.

perspectives.view: Advaita holds that freedom is not produced but recognised: one is already Brahman, and liberation is the removal of ignorance, possible even while living (jivanmukti).
Patanjali describes the goal as kaivalya, the aloneness of pure consciousness when the mind's activity has ceased and it no longer mistakes itself for nature.
Buddhist schools describe nirvana as the extinguishing of craving, aversion and delusion, reached through the Noble Eightfold Path.
Jainism teaches that liberation comes from right faith, right knowledge and right conduct, which stop and destroy karmic matter so the soul rises to its natural omniscience.
In Ramanuja's view the liberated self retains its individuality and enjoys God eternally; freedom comes through devotion, surrender and grace.
Kashmir Shaivism frames liberation as recognition (pratyabhijna) that one's own awareness is Shiva, a freedom that embraces the world rather than escaping it.

startHere.note: Equanimity frees one in this very life; yoga is skill in action. Freedom begins inside everyday work.

goDeeper.note: The one whose happiness and light are within attains the peace of Brahman.
The final teaching: take refuge and do not grieve.
Liberation as purification of the soul.
